title: Going viral: why the message itself must invite retransmission
summary: Jason Cohen uses a Darwinian analogy (the sterile mule) to argue that virality needs "grandchildren": content your followers want to repeat, not just consume. He recommends making retransmission frictionless by writing the share text for people, but admits the real driver is genuinely remarkable content.

principles.text: Virality needs second-generation spread: content must be worth repeating, not just interesting to direct followers.
principles.quote: It's not enough for the message to be interesting to your *direct* followers (children), it needs to be something your followers would be interested in *repeating* (grandchildren).

principles.text: Build the ask for retransmission into the message itself.
principles.quote: The message itself needs to suggest retransmission.

principles.text: Vague requests to 'tell everyone' give people work; remove that friction.
principles.quote: The problem is that you've just given Francis work to do.

principles.text: Do the thinking for your promoters: supply ready-made tweet and email copy tailored to each channel.
principles.quote: Instead, help Francis. Tear down every barrier they have for retransmission. Do the thinking for them.

principles.text: Real virality came from genuinely useful, entertaining or inspiring content, not from sharing tactics.
principles.quote: when my posts have gone viral it wasn't because of these techniques!

principles.text: The number one rule is overwhelmingly good content that people intrinsically want to spread; then also help them share.
principles.quote: So the #1 best rule is: Have overwhelmingly awesome content. So good that people intrinsically want to spread the word.
